extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, meteorologists, botanists, geographers, and scientific readers interested in physical geography and the distribution of organisms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and empirical principles for describing Earth's physical geography, meteorological phenomena, and the spatial distribution of plants and animals, with emphasis on observational methods and instrument limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope when using electrometric observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting itself to results yielded by electrometric observations ... the physical description of the universe should merely notice the incontestable increase of intensity in the general positive electricity of the atmosphere accompanying an increase of altitude and the absence of trees, its daily variations, and its variations in the different seasons of the year, at different distances from the equator, and in the different relations of continental or oceanic surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report altitude-related increase in positive atmospheric electricity, note differences where trees are absent, document daily and seasonal cycles, and compare variations by latitude and by continental versus oceanic contexts; be explicit about the observational scope when relying solely on electrometric data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of land/sea contrast in electric equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: The electric equilibrium is less frequently disturbed where the aerial ocean rests on a liquid base than where it impends over the land; ... small insular groups affect the condition of the atmosphere, and occasion the formation of storms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In meteorological descriptions, explicitly contrast atmospheric electrical behaviour over oceans versus land, and account for effects of islands and insular groups on local storm formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report polarity shifts in fogs and early snow
rubrics_metrics.description: In fogs, and in the commencement of falls of snow ... the previously permanent positive electricity rapidly pass into the negative condition ... The alternate transition was precisely similar to that indicated by the electrometer shortly before and during a storm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting atmospheric electricity during fog or snowfall, record rapid polarity changes and compare electrometer behavior before and during storms; include altitude range of observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental controls for Saussure-type electrometer readings
rubrics_metrics.description: I here only refer to those of my experiments in which the three-foot metallic conductor of Saussure's electrometer was neither moved upward nor downward, nor, according to Volta's proposal, armed with burning sponge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and maintain explicit experimental constraints (e.g., fixed conductor position, no burning sponge) when reporting electrometer results to ensure comparability and to avoid artefacts from instrument manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloud electrification linked to condensation of vapor vesicles
rubrics_metrics.description: When the vesicles of vapor have become condensed into clouds, having definite outlines, the electric tension of the external surface will be increased in proportion to the amount of electricity which passes over to it from the separate vesicles of vapor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute increases in cloud-surface electric tension to condensation processes; in analysis, quantify or qualitatively relate cloud outline/condensation amount to surface tension changes when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloud colour as an empirical indicator of electrical sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Slate-gray clouds are charged, according to Peltier's experiments at Paris, with negative, and white, red, and orange-colored clouds with positive electricity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed cloud coloration as a heuristic for electrical sign, citing experimental sources (e.g., Peltier), but treat as empirical correlation rather than a universal law and compare with other investigators' findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of lightning forms
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Arago's investigations ... the evolution of light (lightning) is of three kinds -- zigzag, and sharply defined at the edges; in sheets of light, illuminating a whole cloud ... ; and in the form of fire-balls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify observed lightning into Arago's three kinds (zigzag, sheet, globular), record durations (two first ~1/1000 second; globular visible for several seconds), and note accompanying meteorological conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document geographic distribution of storms and lightning
rubrics_metrics.description: In the geographical distribution of storms, the Peruvian coast, which is not visited by thunder or lightning, presents the most striking contrast to the rest of the tropical zone ... electric explosions are extremely rare in high northern regions (between 70 degrees and 75 degrees latitude).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mapping storm occurrence, include regional contrasts (e.g., Peruvian coast vs other tropics; high northern latitudes), and rely on navigators' and observational testimony to support distributional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteorology should seek foundation in the torrid zone
rubrics_metrics.description: It has always appeared to me that meteorology must first seek its foundation and progress in the torrid zone, where the variations of the atmospheric pressure, the course of hydro-meteors, and the phenomena of electric explosion, are all of periodic occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize systematic observational programs in the torrid (tropical) zone to establish meteorological foundations, because periodicity there makes processes more tractable for study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument suitability: barometer vs thermometer/psychrometer
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been justly remarked, that it is the barometer alone which indicates to us the changes that occur in the pressure of the air throughout all the aerial strata from the place of observation to the extremest confines of the atmosphere, while the thermometer and psychrometer only acquaint us with all the variations occurring in the local heat and moisture of the lower strata of air in contact with the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the barometer to infer pressure changes across atmospheric strata; recognize thermometers/psychrometers measure only local lower-strata heat and moisture; choose instruments according to the vertical scope of the phenomenon under study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer upper-air thermic and hygrometric modifications via barometric combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The simultaneous thermic and hygrometric modifications of the upper regions of the air can only be learned (when direct observations on mountain stations or aerostatic ascents are impracticable) from hypothetical combinations, by making the barometer serve both as a thermometer and an hygrometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct upper-air measurements are impracticable, use barometer-based hypothetical combinations to infer upper-air temperature and humidity, but acknowledge assumptions and limitations of such inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute important weather changes to distant upper-air disturbances
rubrics_metrics.description: Important changes of weather are not owing to merely local causes, situated at the place of observation, but are the consequence of a disturbance in the equilibrium of the aerial currents at a great distance from the surface of the Earth, in the higher strata of the atmosphere, bringing cold or warm, dry or moist air ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In weather analysis and prediction, account for remote disturbances in high-level aerial currents rather than assuming purely local causation; incorporate regional/upper-air dynamics into explanatory models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation of cosmical history to facts, not origins
rubrics_metrics.description: A cosmical history of the universe, resting upon facts as its basis, has, from the nature and limitations of its sphere, necessarily no connection with the obscure domain embraced by a 'history of organisms', if we understand the word 'history' in its broadest sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When compiling cosmical/physical descriptions, restrict claims to observable facts and avoid speculative narratives about origins or metaphysical 'histories' of organisms beyond empirical foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include inorganic elements and forces relevant to organic tissues
rubrics_metrics.description: The inorganic crust of the Earth contains within it the same elements that enter into the structure of animal and vegetable organs. A physical cosmography would therefore be incomplete if it were to omit a consideration of these forces, and of the substances which enter into solid and fluid combinations in organic tissues ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an interdisciplinary approach: physical cosmography should incorporate chemical/physical elements and forces pertinent to organic structure and vitality to provide a more complete account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor direct observation over deduction for discovering microscopic life
rubrics_metrics.description: Our knowledge of this branch of science has been most remarkably increased by Ehrenberg's brilliant discovery 'on microscopic life ...' -- a discovery based, not on deductive conclusions, but on direct observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize empirical, observational methods (microscopy, sampling) in studies of microscopic life; value specimen collection and direct visual evidence over purely deductive inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize vertical (elevation) repetition of climatic zones
rubrics_metrics.description: Zones of elevation on mountains correspond to parallels of latitude, the higher with the more northern or southern, as the case may be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mapping vegetation and fauna, treat mountain elevation bands as analogues to latitudinal zones; use elevation to predict ecological succession and species assemblages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'representative' vs 'identical' species when applying biogeographical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: When announcing ... that climatic zones of animal and vegetable life are mutually repeated or represented by elevation and latitude, naturalists have not hitherto sufficiently (if at all) distinguished between the evidence of that law, as exhibited by 'representative species' and by 'identical'. In reality, the former essentially depend on the law, the latter being an 'accident' not necessarily dependent upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In explanations of distributional similarity across elevation/latitude, differentiate between different but analogous ('representative') species that demonstrate the general law, and identical species whose presence may be an accidental result requiring separate explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify species change with latitude/elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific treatment of the subject began ... when the arrangement of vegetable forms in natural families admitted of a numerical estimate being made of the different forms which increase or decrease as we recede from the equator toward the poles, and of the relations in which, in different parts of the earth, each family stood with reference to the whole mass of phanerogamic indigenous plants of the same region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerical estimates to document how taxa increase or decrease with latitude/elevation; compare family-level representation regionally and relate counts to isothermal/isochimenal patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'social' plants in biogeographical mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Vital organisms ... may be considered either according to the difference and relative numbers of the types ... or according to the number of individuals of each species on a given area. In the mode of life of plants ... they either exist in an isolated state, or live in a social condition. Those species of plants which I have termed 'social' uniformly cover vast extents of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing plant distributions, distinguish between isolated and 'social' species (those forming extensive uniform covers); assess how social species determine the physiognomy of a district and how human agriculture modifies their predominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for microscopic life in diverse and extreme environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only in the polar regions is there an uninterrupted development of active microscopic life ... Even in the residuum obtained from the melted ice ... there were found upward of fifty species of silicious-shelled Polygastria and Coscinodiscae with their green ovaries, and therefore living and able to resist the extreme severity of the cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sampling from extreme environments (polar ice, deep ocean residue) when assessing global life distribution; do not assume absence of life in ostensibly inhospitable locales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple lines of evidence (narrative testimony, sampling, experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the abundant evidence collected by Arago from the testimony of navigators (Scoresby, Parry, Ross, and Franklin) ... ; Ehrenberg's discoveries ... are based on direct observation ... Peltier's experiments ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine navigators' testimonies, systematic sampling, and controlled experiments to support geographic and meteorological claims; cite sources and reconcile discordant experimental views when possible.
